teacher_notes.title: Communication goal

teacher_notes.title: Lead-in discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask the class: Which jobs will disappear? Give students two minutes in pairs, then take three answers. Do not correct language yet; note useful vocabulary on the board.

teacher_notes.title: Goal discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: 'What can you already do in English connected to jobs then and now? What do you want to be able to do by the end of the lesson?' Write two answers on the board.

teacher_notes.title: Success criteria

teacher_notes.title: Fast finisher

teacher_notes.content: Ask: 'What do you already know about jobs then and now? What would you like to learn today?'

elements.content: Core Active Vocabulary (10 items):

job — the work you do for money.
bank — a place that keeps money. Example: My grandmother used to work in a bank, but she did not use a computer.
computer — an electronic machine for storing and using information. Example: My grandmother used to work in a bank, but she did not use a computer.
software — programs used by a computer. Example: Today, bank workers use software and speak to customers online.
customer /ˈkʌs.tə.mər/ — A person who buys goods from a shop. Example: The store manager helped the happy customer.
disappear — to stop being seen or to no longer exist.
appear /əˈpɪər/ — Come into sight or seem to be true. Example: A rainbow appeared in the sky after the storm.
by hand — using your hands, not a machine. Example: 'I used to write everything by hand,' she says.
office — a room or building where people work.
factory — a building where goods are made.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• What do you do for a living?
• I work as a software developer
• She got promoted last week!
• My grandmother used to work in a bank, but she did not use a computer
• Today, bank workers use software and speak to customers online

teacher_notes.title: 5-step vocabulary progression
teacher_notes.content: 1 Recognition -> 2 Pronunciation -> 3 Matching/classification -> 4 Controlled production -> 5 Personalised use. Keep the pace brisk and check meaning before form.

teacher_notes.title: Meaning check
teacher_notes.content: Ask: 'Which word means ...?' Use the definitions on the slide. Then ask students to cover the definitions and explain three words in their own words.

teacher_notes.title: Discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: What jobs did your grandparents do? Encourage students to use at least three target words in their answers.

teacher_notes.title: Anticipated problems
teacher_notes.content: Watch for pronunciation problems in job, bank, computer. Drill the words chorally and individually before the practice.

teacher_notes.title: Extension
teacher_notes.content: Ask students to categorise the ten words into 'people', 'actions' and 'things', then compare categories with a partner.

teacher_notes.title: Drill script
teacher_notes.content: Model each word twice. Use choral repetition, then individual repetition. Ask students to tap the stressed syllable. Finish with the sentence drill: 'What do you do for a living?'.

teacher_notes.title: Discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: 'Which words are difficult for you? Why?' Let students compare first language sounds with English sounds.

teacher_notes.title: Peer discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask pairs to choose the two hardest words and agree on one tip for saying them. Take two tips from the class.

teacher_notes.title: Error correction
teacher_notes.content: Correct only the target feature during the drill. Note other errors for delayed feedback at the end of the lesson.

elements.content: Grammar Focus: use Used To: Past Habits & Past States, Past Simple Review to talk about jobs then and now.

Form:
Affirmative: subject + used to + base verb.
Negative: subject + didn't use to + base verb.
Question: Did + subject + use to + base verb?

Regular verbs: base verb + -ed. Irregular verbs: learn the past form (go -> went).
Negatives and questions use did/didn't + base verb.

Examples:
• I used to play football every weekend.
• She didn't use to like coffee.
• I moved to this city three years ago.
• She didn't go to the party last night.
Controlled practice: check the meaning and form.
Is the habit true now?
Do we say 'didn't used to'?
Is the action finished?
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I used to play football every weekend.
• Now change the subject and the time.
• Now make a question.
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• Which jobs will disappear?
• What jobs did your grandparents do?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences on the topic 'jobs then and now' using the target structure.
• Write one question to ask your partner.

teacher_notes.title: Function-first grammar rule
teacher_notes.content: Frame the grammar as a communicative tool, not an abstract rule: Used To: Past Habits & Past States, Past Simple Review helps learners talk about jobs then and now.

teacher_notes.title: CCQs
teacher_notes.content: Is the habit true now? (No.) Do we say 'didn't used to'? (No, 'didn't use to'.)

teacher_notes.title: Discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: Are new jobs better than old jobs? Push students to justify their answers with a full sentence using the target grammar.

teacher_notes.title: Common errors
teacher_notes.content: 'didn't used to' -> 'didn't use to'. Using 'used to' for a single past event: 'I used to visit Rome in 2019' -> 'I visited Rome in 2019'. Using the past form after 'didn't': 'didn't went' -> 'didn't go'.

teacher_notes.title: Extension
teacher_notes.content: Ask students to transform two sentences into a question and a negative, then check with a partner.

elements.content: Reading: Old jobs, new jobs

My grandmother used to work in a bank, but she did not use a computer. Today, bank workers use software and speak to customers online. Some old jobs have disappeared, and new jobs have appeared. 'I used to write everything by hand,' she says.
My grandmother used to work in a ___, but she did not use a computer.
Today, ___ workers use software and speak to customers online.
What is the text mainly about?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Have you heard the news about Sarah?
B: Yes! She got promoted to senior manager after her excellent annual review.

teacher_notes.title: Skills focus
teacher_notes.content: Listening (~10%) + Reading (~10%). The reading gives context; the dialogue models the target chunks in a real exchange.

teacher_notes.title: Pre-reading discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: What job would you like to try? Set a purpose for reading: 'Read to find out what the person says about jobs then and now.'

teacher_notes.title: Comprehension check
teacher_notes.content: Students answer alone, then compare in pairs. Check answers with the whole class and ask students to justify them from the text.

teacher_notes.title: Post-reading discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: 'Do you agree with the person in the text? Why or why not?' Use the target vocabulary in the discussion.

elements.content: Speaking task: discuss the topic 'jobs then and now' with your partner. Use at least five target words and the target grammar.

• Which jobs will disappear?
• What jobs did your grandparents do?
• Are new jobs better than old jobs?
• What job would you like to try?
Adult speaking frames:

• I used to ..., but now I ...
• Did you use to ... when you were younger?
• Things were very different when I was ...
Role-play card: Which jobs will disappear?

Student A: You have a strong view on 'Which jobs will disappear?'. Explain your opinion with two reasons and one example from your own life.

Student B: You partly disagree. Ask one follow-up question, then give a different view using the target language.

Swap roles after four minutes.
Writing task: write a short message (60-80 words) to a friend or colleague about 'jobs then and now'. Use the target grammar and at least five target words.
Model: My grandmother used to work in a bank, but she did not use a computer. Today, bank workers use software and speak to customers online. Use the target grammar and at least five target words.
Peer check: swap your message with a partner. Underline one sentence you like and one verb form to check. Then ask one spoken question about your partner's text.

teacher_notes.title: Speaking aim (~70%)
teacher_notes.content: Fluency first, accuracy second. Give students 6-8 minutes for the pair task, then ask two pairs to report back.

teacher_notes.title: Monitoring focus
teacher_notes.content: Monitor for the target grammar and the ten target words. Note three good sentences and three errors for delayed feedback.

teacher_notes.title: Discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask the class: 'Which jobs will disappear?' and 'What jobs did your grandparents do?' Encourage students to respond to each other, not just to you.

teacher_notes.title: Feedback discussion
teacher_notes.content: After the role-play, ask: 'Which question produced the most interesting answer? Why?' Invite two pairs to share one answer with the class.

teacher_notes.title: Speaking frames discussion
teacher_notes.content: Put the three frames on the board. Ask students which frame is most useful for their own life and why. Drill the frames chorally, then let students personalise them.

teacher_notes.title: Role-play setup
teacher_notes.content: Assign A and B. Give A one minute to prepare two reasons. Give B one minute to prepare one question and a different view. Monitor for the target grammar and the ten target words.

teacher_notes.title: Writing support
teacher_notes.content: Give students 6 minutes to write 60-80 words. Remind them to use the model, the frames, and at least five target words.

teacher_notes.title: Peer-check discussion
teacher_notes.content: Pairs swap messages, underline one strong sentence and one verb form to check, then ask one spoken question about the text. Take two examples of good language from the class.

teacher_notes.title: Extension
teacher_notes.content: Ask fast finishers to turn their message into a short spoken update and deliver it to another pair.

elements.content: Timestamped Multi-Duration Flows:

• 60 min (Essential): 0-8 Warm-up & goal; 8-18 Vocabulary & chunks; 18-28 Grammar & controlled practice; 28-40 Reading/listening + speaking; 40-50 Role-play; 50-60 Cool-down & homework.

• 90 min (Expanded): 0-10 Warm-up; 10-25 Vocabulary & pronunciation; 25-40 Grammar & controlled practice; 40-55 Reading/listening; 55-70 Speaking task; 70-85 Writing & feedback; 85-90 Cool-down.

• 120 min (Full Workshop): 0-15 Warm-up & discussion; 15-35 Vocabulary & pronunciation lab; 35-60 Grammar workshop; 60-80 Reading/listening & language focus; 80-100 Speaking role-play; 100-115 Writing & portfolio; 115-120 Feedback & homework.

teacher_notes.title: Multi-duration strategy
teacher_notes.content: Choose the 60, 90 or 120-minute flow before the lesson. The core is the same; the expanded versions add practice and feedback, not new grammar.

teacher_notes.title: Timing discussion
teacher_notes.content: If time is short, cut the writing task to two sentences and keep the speaking task. If time is long, add the extension on slide 7.

teacher_notes.title: Discussion
teacher_notes.content: Ask: 'Which part of this lesson do you need most practice in: vocabulary, grammar or speaking?' Use the answer to choose the longer flow.

teacher_notes.title: Planning note
teacher_notes.content: The 60-minute flow is the minimum for a complete lesson. Do not skip the recycling or the speaking task; they carry the communicative goal.
